name: Aman, who ensnared Achiacharus
charge: Treachery against the man who brought him up
summary: Achiacharus was Tobit’s brother’s son, cupbearer, keeper of the signet, steward and overseer of the accounts under the king at Nineveh, and it was he who interceded for Tobit and brought him home, and who nourished him while he was blind (Tobit 1:21-22; Tobit 2:10). Tobit’s dying counsel holds up one case against that kindness: remember how Aman handled Achiacharus who brought him up, how out of light he brought him into darkness, and how he was rewarded for it (Tobit 14:10). Achiacharus was saved, and the man who laid the snare fell into it and perished.
offenseFull: The record first shows Achiacharus in office. He was Anael’s son, Tobit’s brother’s son, and the king set him next to himself as cupbearer, keeper of the signet, steward and overseer of the accounts, and he entreated for Tobit so that Tobit could return to Nineveh after his goods had been seized and his life sought for burying the dead (Tobit 1:21-22). When Tobit was blinded, it was Achiacharus who nourished him until he went into Elymais (Tobit 2:10). Everything the man had, Aman had from him. That is the weight of the charge. The teaching on this chapter puts it in one line: you do good and good follows you, you do evil and evil follows you. The injury was not hostility between strangers; it was the return made for the care that had raised him.

Tobit sets the case down at the very end of his life, in the middle of his charge to his son to keep the law and the commandments and to show himself merciful (Tobit 14:9-10). He does not tell the story for its own sake. He tells it as the counterweight to the instruction, because a son who has just been told to be merciful and just needs also to be told what it looks like when a man takes kindness and turns it into an opportunity. The whole book has been arguing that alms and righteousness are what a man is measured by, and here is the man who was fed by another man’s righteousness and used it against him.
judgmentFull: Aman brought his benefactor out of light into darkness, and the reward came back on him: Achiacharus was saved, and the other had his reward, for he went down into darkness (Tobit 14:10). Tobit names the pattern twice over in the same breath, setting Manasses, who gave alms and escaped the snare of death, beside Aman, who fell into the snare and perished (Tobit 14:10). The same two ends are what the wisdom of the fathers teaches about a pit dug for another man and a net laid in secret (Proverbs 26:27; Psalms 35:7-8), and the deliverance of Achiacharus is of a piece with the deliverance of Tobit himself, who was restored and whose nephew came to rejoice with him (Tobit 11:18).

Tobit draws the conclusion himself and gives it to his son as the last thing he says before he dies: consider what alms do, and how righteousness delivers (Tobit 14:11). The teaching on the chapter reads the case exactly that way, as a father’s final advice rather than a story about a villain. The betrayer did not obtain what he intended. The man he wronged lived, the snare took its own maker, and the lesson set beside the charge to keep the law and be merciful is that a man is not saved by his position at the king’s right hand but by what he does with the mercy he has received.

lawsResolved.text: You shall not deal falsely or treacherously with your brethren.
Punishment will come to those who attempt to gain by deceit.
Punishment is the fruit and reward for iniquity and wicked ways (you shall reap that which you sow).

text.text: And there passed not five and fifty days, before two of his sons killed him, and they fled into the mountains of Ararath; and Sarchedonus his son reigned in his stead; who appointed over his father’s accounts, and over all his affairs, Achiacharus my brother Anael’s son.

And Achiacharus intreating for me, I returned to Nineve. Now Achiacharus was cupbearer, and keeper of the signet, and steward, and overseer of the accounts: and Sarchedonus appointed him next unto him: and he was my brother’s son.

And I knew not that there were sparrows in the wall, and mine eyes being open, the sparrows muted warm dung into mine eyes, and a whiteness came in mine eyes: and I went to the physicians, but they helped me not: moreover Achiacharus did nourish me, until I went into Elymais.

And bury me decently, and thy mother with me; but tarry no longer at Nineve. Remember, my son, how Aman handled Achiacharus that brought him up, how out of light he brought him into darkness, and how he rewarded him again: yet Achiacharus was saved, but the other had his reward: for he went down into darkness. Manasses gave alms, and escaped the snares of death which they had set for him: but Aman fell into the snare, and perished.

Wherefore now, my son, consider what alms doeth, and how righteousness doth deliver. When he had said these things, he gave up the ghost in the bed, being an hundred and eight and fifty years old; and he buried him honourably.
Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him.
For without cause have they hid for me their net in a pit, which without cause they have digged for my soul.
Let destruction come upon him at unawares; and let his net that he hath hid catch himself: into that very destruction let him fall.
And Achiacharus, and Nasbas his brother’s son, came:
